method: Five independent read-only lenses over the waves 1-7 surfaces, each finding then subjected to an adversarial refutation pass whose default verdict is refuted.

candidateFindings.title: Recovery rehearsal "human pause" is bound to an arbitrary file and leaves no trace in the evidence
candidateFindings.failureScenario: An operator runs only `--apply`. They pass `--plan-file=/tmp/anything.txt` (never produced by `--plan`, never parsed as a plan), compute `sha256` of that file themselves, and write `authorization.json` with `planSha256` set to it, `operator` = their own id, any `reason`. `runApplyMode` computes `planSha256 = releaseEvidenceSha256(planDocument)` at line 268 with no schema check, the digest matches, `recoveryRehearsalTransition` advances through `execute`, and a `passed` `promotion.restore_rollback` artifact is emitted. Because `recoveryRehearsalDependencyDigests` (src/shared/release/recovery-rehearsal-evidence.ts:303-344) names neither the plan digest nor the authorization digest, `assembleRecoveryRehearsalEvidence` filters both out of its returned `dependencies` (recovery-rehearsal-plan.ts:561-568), so neither file is written to the dependency dir and Gate F sees no evidence that any plan or authorization ever existed. The claimed 'plan → authorize → execute' separation collapses into one self-attested invocation.
candidateFindings.evidence: scripts/release/rehearse-recovery.ts:227-268 reads `--plan-file` as an opaque string and never calls `parseCanonicalReleaseEvidence` or any plan schema; the candidate inside the plan is never compared to the candidate in `--observations`. src/shared/release/recovery-rehearsal-evidence.ts contains no occurrence of `planSha256` or `authorization` (grep returns nothing), and `recoveryRehearsalDependencyDigests` lists only operator-supplied read-back references. src/shared/release/recovery-rehearsal-plan.ts:561-568 returns `digests.map(...)` — the plan and authorization files supplied at rehearse-recovery.ts:304-308 are silently dropped. The module header at recovery-rehearsal-plan.ts:8-13 claims "MANDATORY HUMAN PAUSE, KEYED TO THE PLAN DIGEST … the thing that was approved and the thing that runs are the same bytes." scripts/release/rehearse-recovery.test.ts has no case feeding a non-plan file as `--plan-file`, and its retention test (line 314-320) only iterates `recoveryRehearsalDependencyDigests`, so it cannot notice the plan being dropped.
candidateFindings.lens: Evidence integrity — whether the new REL-01/LEG-01/Gate F machinery can produce evidence for something that did not happen

candidateFindings.title: Gate F role separation ("engineering cannot sign for counsel") is declared but never enforced
candidateFindings.failureScenario: Enrol the same Ed25519 public key (same `publicKeyPem` / `publicKeySha256`) under both `security` and `counsel` in `security/gate-f-approval-roles.json`. `roleKeyMapSchema` (lines 125-144) has no `superRefine` and no distinctness constraint, so the map parses. `createGateFApprovalVerifier` (lines 236-277) only checks `envelope.publicKeySha256 === roleKeys.roles[envelope.role].publicKeySha256`, so one key holder signs both the `security` and the `counsel` payloads and both verify `ok: true`. Gate F then reports a validly-signed counsel approval for a release counsel never saw. Separately, `approverIdentity` is never compared to the role key's `custodian`, and `LEGAL_SELF_APPROVAL_PROHIBITED` (src/shared/governance/legal-approval-authority.ts:38) is not applied to Gate F approvers, so the counsel envelope may carry the operator's own name.
candidateFindings.evidence: `GATE_F_ENGINEERING_ROLES` is exported at src/shared/release/gate-f-approval-envelope.ts:54 with the comment "None of them may stand in for counsel", and `grep -rn GATE_F_ENGINEERING_ROLES` over the whole repo returns exactly that one declaration line — no consumer, no test. `security/gate-f-approval-roles.json` asserts in its `operations` note that "role separation is enforced structurally by the signed payload's role field", but the role field only selects which enrolled key is looked up. The only test that touches this, src/shared/release/gate-f-approval-envelope.test.ts:203 ('are the sha256 of the SPKI DER, so two roles cannot share an identity'), asserts distinctness of six keys the fixture itself generated — it would still pass if the production map enrolled one key for all six roles.
candidateFindings.lens: Evidence integrity — whether the new REL-01/LEG-01/Gate F machinery can produce evidence for something that did not happen

candidateFindings.title: Gate F accepts a bundle where the approved legal bytes and the on-disk legal bytes disagree
candidateFindings.failureScenario: `docs/legal/privacy-notice.md` is edited after counsel approval. The registry row (and therefore every `release.legalRevisionSet` entry, which is copied field-by-field from it) still carries the pre-edit digest A. The `release.legalApprovalChecklist` honestly records the post-edit on-disk digest B. `parseLegalRevisionSetEvidence` only compares entry.sha256 to the registry row (legal-revision-set-evidence.ts:192-194) and never reads the file; `parseLegalApprovalChecklist` only compares its own document digests to `readDocument(path)` (legal-approval-checklist.ts:275-303) and never looks at the registry. `validateGateFEvidenceBundle`'s single cross-check on the checklist (gate-f-evidence.ts:742-756) compares only `legalRevisionSetSha256`. The bundle validates, and counsel/founder sign `legalRevisionSetSha256`, which covers digest A while the shipped document is B.
candidateFindings.evidence: gate-f-evidence.ts:742-756 is the entire cross-artifact check on the checklist. The doc comment at gate-f-evidence.ts:140-146 claims the two together prove "WHICH legal bytes counsel approved" plus that "the approval is still current" — but the documentId sets are identical (LEGAL_CHECKLIST_DOCUMENTS in legal-approval-checklist.ts:48-58 vs LEGAL_PUBLICATION_DOCUMENT_IDS in legal-approval-authority.ts:47-51) and their per-document `sha256` fields are never compared. The fixture src/shared/release/gate-f-complete-evidence.test-fixtures.ts:260-268 derives the checklist digests from its own document bytes, independent of the registry rows the revision set mirrors, so the test suite would not catch divergence. Mitigated only by `pnpm check:legal-registry` (package.json:30, lint:ci), which is a separate CI job on the repo checkout, not part of Gate F bundle validation.

candidateFindings.title: Gate F legal-approval-checklist facts are pure self-attestation; an open blocking counsel decision does not block the gate
candidateFindings.failureScenario: Hand-write a `repkey-legal-approval-checklist-1` JSON with the 13 `LEG_01_REQUIRED_FACT_KEYS`, each `decided: true`, `decision: "counsel decided X"`, `decidedBy: "A. Counsel"`, `sourceDocumentId: "privacy-notice"`, `checklistItemIds: ["anything"]`. candidateFindings.title: Canary continuity counters record zero for identity fields no source ever reports
candidateFindings.failureScenario: `observeCanaryWindow` increments `releaseIdentityMismatches` only when `reading.identity.releaseSha`/`releaseManifestSha256` is `!== undefined` and differs. `identityFrom` in scripts/release/observe-canary-window.ts:133-149 can only extract `releaseManifestSha256` if the body exposes it, and the two non-overridable sources are `/api/health/metrics` and `/api/health/ready`, whose OperationsSnapshot exposes `release: { sha }` only (src/shared/health/operations-snapshot.ts:288) — no manifest digest. The emitted artifact therefore asserts `continuity.releaseIdentityMismatches: 0` and satisfies the `passing` predicate in canary-window-evidence.ts:243-250, when in fact the manifest half of release identity was never compared at all. The same shape applies to `configurationHeadMismatches`: only sources that volunteer a `versions` object are compared, and a single one suffices.
candidateFindings.evidence: src/shared/release/canary-sampler.ts:230-251 — both mismatch counters are guarded on the field being present, and an absent field is silently treated as agreement rather than as a missing sample (contrast lines 206-217, where an unreadable sample is correctly recorded as missing and forces failure). canary-window-evidence.ts:243-250 then reads those zeros as proof of continuity. The module header at canary-sampler.ts:6 states the rule "UNAVAILABLE DATA IS FAILURE, NOT ABSENCE", which holds for sample values but not for these two continuity signals.

candidateFindings.title: The role-key enrolment procedure the shipped key map documents does not exist

candidateFindings.title: The backup-erasure ledger lives inside the database it is meant to fence, so a PITR restore erases the very entries the fence must replay
candidateFindings.failureScenario: Property P is erased on day 10; the erasure and its ledger row commit in the same transaction (advance-property-erase.job.ts:183). An incident on day 12 forces a PITR restore of the US cell to day 8. The restore rolls the whole database back, so P's rows are back AND the day-10 ledger row is gone. `applyRestoreResurrectionFence(tx, {dataCellId:'us', restorePointAt: day8, replayers})` calls `readBackupErasureLedger(tx, 'us')` against that same restored connection, gets no entry for the erasure, produces an empty plan, and returns `{verified: true, ledgerEntriesConsidered: 0, ...}`. `assertRestoredCellVerified` passes. The erased Property is served again with no signal anywhere. By construction `planBackupErasureReplay` can only classify an entry `replay_required` when `effectiveErasureAt > restorePointAt` (line 282) — and every such entry was written after the restore point, so it cannot exist in a cell restored to that point. The one disposition the fence exists to produce is unreachable in a real restore.
candidateFindings.evidence: backup-erasure-ledger.ts:140-174 appends inside the erasure's own `Tx` (header lines 4-9 make this explicit and call it load-bearing). drizzle/0172_backup_erasure_ledger.sql creates `backup_erasure_ledger` as an ordinary table in the tenant database — no separate cluster, no logical replication, no export. `readBackupErasureLedger(tx, dataCellId)` at line 240 and `applyRestoreResurrectionFence(tx, ...)` at line 358 take a single `Tx`, so the ledger is read from the same restored connection the replayers write to. `grep -rn 'appendBackupErasureLedgerEntry|readBackupErasureLedger' src scripts docs` finds no out-of-cell copy or pre-restore export anywhere. docs/operations/backup-and-lifecycle.md:398-465 never addresses the ledger's own survival across the restore.
candidateFindings.lens: Irreversible data loss: the 17 Organization purge contributors, permanent Property Erase, privacy erasure, the backup-erasure ledger + restore resurrection fence, and the retention registry.

candidateFindings.title: Organization purge writes no backup-erasure ledger entry at all, so the only registered replayer targets a subject class nothing produces
candidateFindings.failureScenario: An Organization is purged: all 16 composed contributors run their destructive phases and each co-commits a content-free receipt. No `backup_erasure_ledger` row is written for any of them. A later restore to a point before the purge therefore has nothing to replay even if the ledger survived — the resurrected Organization is invisible to the fence. Conversely, `createGuestBackupErasureReplayer` is registered for `(context:'guest', subjectClass:'organization')`, a pair no producer ever emits, so the single existing replayer is dead code.
candidateFindings.evidence: The scaffold at organization-lifecycle-receipt-store.ts:234-247 runs the phase work and inserts only `contextOrganizationLifecycleReceipts` — no ledger append. None of the 16 adapters under src/contexts/*/infrastructure/adapters/*-organization-lifecycle.adapter.ts imports `#/shared/db/lifecycle/backup-erasure-ledger` (verified by grep). `grep -rn "subjectClass: 'organization'" src | grep -v test` returns exactly one hit: guest-backup-erasure-replayer.adapter.ts:33, the consumer. docs/operations/backup-and-lifecycle.md:419 claims the opposite: "Organization purge (LIF-01-T14) | organization | closure lineage, one entry per context plan".
candidateFindings.lens: Irreversible data loss: the 17 Organization purge contributors, permanent Property Erase, privacy erasure, the backup-erasure ledger + restore resurrection fence, and the retention registry.

candidateFindings.title: Nothing calls the restore resurrection fence, and restore-verify's own cutover checklist omits it
candidateFindings.failureScenario: An operator runs `pnpm ops:restore-verify --apply` inside the isolated restored environment — the documented, and only, production restore verification path. It sweeps retention, applies `applyRecoveryFence`, prints "✓ zero unfenced restored authority remains — recovery fence verified" and then a six-step cutover checklist. Neither `applyRestoreResurrectionFence` nor `assertRestoredCellVerified` is called, and no checklist step mentions the erasure ledger. The operator follows the tool's own output, unsets RESTORE_MODE, and opens a cell that has resurrected every purged tenant, erased Property and privacy subject.
candidateFindings.evidence: `grep -rn 'applyRestoreResurrectionFence|assertRestoredCellVerified' src scripts` finds only backup-erasure-ledger.ts (definition), recovery-fence.ts:113 (definition), and two test files. postgres-recovery-fence.ts:155-712 does not touch the ledger. restore-verify.ts:331-376 runs `applyRecoveryFence` and prints steps 1-6 with no resurrection-fence step. docs/operations/backup-and-lifecycle.md:463 admits "Wiring not yet composed", but docs/release-evidence/review/comprehensive-program-status-2026-08-26.json:1369 claims "The backup-erasure ledger and restore resurrection fence stop a restore from undoing a purge".

candidateFindings.title: The retention registry's counsel-approval gate is never applied to the rules that actually execute; the daily sweep already deletes pending_counsel classes
candidateFindings.failureScenario: `createRetentionSweepHandler` checks `assertRetentionRegistryApplyAllowed` only over `deps.registryApplyRules` — an optional, separately supplied list. The rules it actually runs are `deps.rules ?? RETENTION_RULES`, which are never checked against the registry. Every production caller (scripts/ops/restore-verify.ts:69 passes `rules: RETENTION_RULES` and no `registryApplyRules`; the scheduled worker uses the default) therefore executes destructively with the gate satisfied vacuously. Concretely, the enabled daily job deletes rows for classes the registry marks `pending_counsel` with open counsel decisions: `guest_responses.deidentified_fact` (registry rule `guest.deidentified_facts`, two blocking decisions), `guest_response_private_feedback.expired` (`guest.private_feedback_text`), `notifications` (`notification.delivery_records`), `recent_activity_entries` (`activity.recent_activity`). Adding any further pending rule to RETENTION_RULES arms it with no gate to trip.
candidateFindings.evidence: retention-sweep.job.ts:320-322 gates only `deps.registryApplyRules ?? []`; lines 311 and 388-393 execute `deps.rules ?? RETENTION_RULES` via `executeRetentionRule` with no registry lookup. execute-retention-rule.ts never imports the registry. src/shared/db/retention/retention-registry.ts:12-17 claims "every rule is pending_counsel and assertRetentionRegistryApplyAllowed refuses apply for all of them. Report-only is the only reachable mode" — contradicted by its own `implementedBoundary` strings at lines 320 and 340 ("Live: the scheduled subject ... deletes"). event-job-catalogue.ts:2816-2823 shows retention-sweep with `registration: 'enabled'` on a 24h schedule. retention-registry.test.ts asserts contraction-candidate and horizon invariants against RETENTION_RULES but never asserts approvalState for an executed rule.
candidateFindings.lens: Irreversible data loss: the 17 Organization purge contributors, permanent Property Erase, privacy erasure, the backup-erasure ledger + restore resurrection fence, and the retention registry.

candidateFindings.title: The scheduled guest_responses purge has no lifetime-aggregate ordering gate, permanently stranding undelivered corrections
candidateFindings.failureScenario: A Guest submits a correction or withdrawal whose outbox fact is still unpublished (consumer lag, quarantined queue, a recovery-fenced row). The daily sweep runs `guest_responses.deidentified_fact` with the sole predicate `retention_deadline < now()` and deletes the source facts. The correction can now never reach `portal_metric_lifetime_aggregates`: the aggregate keeps the uncorrected contribution and the fact that would have fixed it no longer exists. The registry's own text calls this out — "the aggregate keeps a contribution whose source is gone and can never be reconciled again" — yet the executable rule enforces nothing.
candidateFindings.evidence: retention-sweep.job.ts:93-98 defines the rule with only `tsColumn: 'retention_deadline'` and no `extraWhere`; executeRetentionRule adds nothing. retention-registry.ts:340 states "Corrections and withdrawals must reach portal_metric_lifetime_aggregates before this purge runs", and lines 369-371 name the ordering constraint as "the operative control". Both other paths that delete the same rows DO enforce it: guest-organization-lifecycle.adapter.ts:284-288 throws GUEST_PURGE_READINESS_BLOCKED on unpublished Guest outbox facts, and metric-organization-lifecycle.adapter.ts:212-224 blocks on aggregate parity. No trigger guards `guest_responses` DELETE (grep over drizzle/*.sql finds only contact-retirement and staff-attribution triggers).
candidateFindings.lens: Irreversible data loss: the 17 Organization purge contributors, permanent Property Erase, privacy erasure, the backup-erasure ledger + restore resurrection fence, and the retention registry.

candidateFindings.title: Privacy erasure deletes source facts before delivering aggregate corrections, inverting the ordering its own contract declares — and the test pins the wrong order
candidateFindings.failureScenario: For an erasure request, `contributor.erase(tx, scope)` runs first (line 265) and destroys the subject's source facts; only then does `deliverAggregateCorrections(tx, scope)` run (line 271). A production implementation that derives the aggregate delta from those source rows now finds nothing to deliver, returns `undelivered: 0`, the gate passes, the ledger entry is appended and the transaction commits — with the erased subject's contributions still baked into `portal_metric_lifetime_aggregates` forever. The gate can only ever fire for the `correct`/`withdraw` operations, which are exactly the ones that do not destroy their own inputs.
candidateFindings.evidence: The function's own contract at privacy-request-lifecycle.ts:208-214 states "1. apply the contributor operation; 2. deliver the resulting corrections; 3. only THEN purge source facts", and the module header at lines 3-9 says "a withdrawal or a correction must reach the anonymous lifetime aggregate BEFORE the source facts are purged". The code does erase→deliver. privacy-request-lifecycle.test.ts:270-274 asserts `['guest.erase','deliverAggregateCorrections','appendLedgerEntry']` under a comment (lines 267-269) that states the very reason this order is wrong. No production `deliverAggregateCorrections` implementation exists yet (grep finds only the test double), so the hazard is latent rather than presently firing.
candidateFindings.lens: Irreversible data loss: the 17 Organization purge contributors, permanent Property Erase, privacy erasure, the backup-erasure ledger + restore resurrection fence, and the retention registry.

candidateFindings.title: Property Erase authority is loaded by id alone, unscoped from the operator's authorized --org/--property
candidateFindings.failureScenario: An operator whose command scope was authorized for Organization A / Property P invokes `preview`, `confirm` or `cancel` with `authority=<id belonging to Organization B>`. `loadAuthority` selects purely on `authorityId` and every downstream step uses `authority.organizationId`/`authority.propertyId` from the loaded row, never `ctx.organizationId`/`ctx.propertyId`. A mistyped or copy-pasted authority id therefore drives an irreversible erasure of a different tenant's Property under an authorization granted for another one, with no mismatch error.
candidateFindings.evidence: erase-property.ts:291-300 `loadAuthority` calls `deps.store.load(authorityId)` with no tenant predicate; confirmPropertyErase (line 231) and cancelPropertyErase (line 280) both use it and never compare against an operator scope. planPropertyEraseCommand (property-erase-command.ts:100-108, 162-164) validates that `--org`, `--property` and `authority=` are all present but never that they agree. Currently unreachable: scripts/ops/property-erase.ts:58-63 refuses every non-report mode with "erase execution is not armed in this build", so this is a latent defect that arming would expose.
candidateFindings.lens: Irreversible data loss: the 17 Organization purge contributors, permanent Property Erase, privacy erasure, the backup-erasure ledger + restore resurrection fence, and the retention registry.

candidateFindings.title: Restore resurrection fence reads the ledger from the very database the restore rolled back, so it can never find an entry to replay
candidateFindings.failureScenario: Cell purges Organization X at 14:00 (appendBackupErasureLedgerEntry commits row with effective_erasure_at = 14:00 inside the purge transaction). At 20:00 the cell is PITR-restored to 12:00. X's rows are back. The operator follows docs/operations/backup-and-lifecycle.md step 3 and runs applyRestoreResurrectionFence(tx, {restorePointAt: 12:00}). readBackupErasureLedger runs `SELECT ... FROM backup_erasure_ledger` through the same Tx -> the same restored Postgres -> the 14:00 row was inserted after 12:00 and was rolled back with everything else, so it is not returned. planBackupErasureReplay sees only rows with effective_erasure_at <= 12:00 and classifies every one of them 'already_erased'. The fence returns verified:true, ledgerEntriesReapplied:0, unreplayedEntryIds:[]. assertRestoredCellVerified passes and the cell is opened with the erased Organization readable again — the exact outcome the control exists to prevent.
candidateFindings.evidence: applyRestoreResurrectionFence (line 371-373) calls readBackupErasureLedger(tx, ...) which at lines 240-246 queries `backup_erasure_ledger` through the caller's Tx. The only definition of that table is src/shared/db/schema/backup-erasure-ledger.schema.ts:95 / drizzle/0172_backup_erasure_ledger.sql (referenced from src/shared/db/schema/db-only-constructs.ts:490) — the application database. `grep -rn 'backup_erasure_ledger' --include=*.ts --include=*.md --include=*.sql .` returns no export, replication, off-cell copy or second connection anywhere. effective_erasure_at is set to the erasure transaction's `now` (advance-property-erase.job.ts:188 passes effectiveErasureAt: now in the same tx as the deletes), so effective time == commit time; every row needing replay is by construction a row written after the restore point. The companion fence it is procedurally paired with, src/shared/db/recovery/postgres-recovery-fence.ts:68/156, also takes the application `Database`. The integration test at src/shared/db/lifecycle/backup-erasure-ledger.integration.test.ts:139-165 hand-builds a state a real restore cannot produce — it inserts the ledger entry AND leaves the guest rows present in one live transaction, then passes restorePointAt = ERASED_AT - 60s — so it would pass identically whether or not the control can work in production.
candidateFindings.lens: Concurrency, idempotence and crash recovery

candidateFindings.title: Export `delete_pending` is an unrecoverable dead end: a crash or transient S3 error between the claim and the delete strands the tenant archive in the bucket forever
candidateFindings.failureScenario: purgeNextExpired calls claimNextExpiredDeletion, which COMMITS the row into state='delete_pending' in its own transaction (line 469-503). Control returns to organization-export.ts:286, `await deps.storage.delete(objectKey)` gets a 503/throttle from S3 (or the pod is killed). The exception propagates; completeDeletion never runs. The row is now delete_pending and the archive is still in the bucket. On every subsequent pass claimNextExpiredDeletion filters `inArray(state, ['ready','retrieval_issued','retrieved'])`, which excludes delete_pending, so the row is never selected again; no other statement in the file touches delete_pending except completeDeletion, which needs an id and expectedRevision only the lost in-memory object had. Result: the full tenant export ZIP stays readable in the private bucket permanently, long past its <=7-day object_expires_at, and the DB row is stuck.
candidateFindings.evidence: claimNextExpiredDeletion state filter at lines 475-479; completeDeletion requires state 'delete_pending' at line 521. The three steps are three separate transactions with the storage call between them (organization-export.ts:282-292). There is no lease to expire: organization_lifecycle.schema.ts:325 requires `generation_lease_expires_at IS NULL` for delete_pending, and organization_exports_generation_idx / claimNextGeneration only ever reclaim 'generating' and 'egress_pending'. Grepping every `.update(organizationExports)` in the repo returns exactly the 8 sites in this file — none re-selects delete_pending. There is no storage-side backstop either: `deleteAfter` is written only as inert S3 user metadata (`Metadata: {'delete-after': ...}`, organization-export-s3-storage.ts:53), not an Expires header, object-expiration tag or bucket lifecycle rule, and no bucket lifecycle configuration exists in the repo. The same dead-end applies to `failed` rows that carry an object_key (allowed by organization_export_state_shape at schema line 341-347): claimNextExpiredDeletion excludes 'failed', so an archive uploaded by a stalled worker after recoverEgress already failed the row is likewise never deleted.
candidateFindings.lens: Concurrency, idempotence and crash recovery

candidateFindings.title: Lifecycle runPhase opens 17 concurrent pool transactions on a 10-connection pool, violating the pinned per-job budget the worker test claims to enforce
candidateFindings.failureScenario: advance-organization-lifecycle runs on the `background` queue (event-job-catalogue.ts:2933). runScheduledPass processes up to 50 candidates; for each it calls runPhase, which fires Promise.all over all 17 ORGANIZATION_LIFECYCLE_CONTEXTS, and every scaffold contributor opens its own deps.db.transaction. That is 17 simultaneous pool checkouts against POOL_MAX_CONNECTIONS = 10, for the whole duration of the pass. All 17 also block on `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` of the SAME organization_lifecycle_authority row while holding their clients, so 9 of the 10 clients sit idle-blocked while one does work. REFUTED. The claim rests on the premise that `contributor.erase` destroys the source facts `deliverAggregateCorrections` would need. The only real implementation of the port in this repo does the opposite, deliberately.

/Users/bozhidardenev/kodes/projects/rep-key/src/contexts/guest/infrastructure/adapters/guest-privacy-subject.adapter.ts (`erase`) deletes reveal audits, contact requests and private feedback, then UPDATEs `guest_responses` to null the rating and consent flags — and its comment states outright that `status` and `deleted_at` are deliberately NOT touched because marking the row deleted "would remove it from the projection that rebuilds the anonymous lifetime aggregate, which is the one thing an erasure must leave standing." The port doc is likewise scoped: "Irreversible purge of the subject's content and contact" — not of the content-free metric fact. This is pinned by an integration test at /Users/bozhidardenev/kodes/projects/rep-key/src/contexts/guest/infrastructure/adapters/guest-privacy-subject.adapter.integration.test.ts:274-317, which asserts after erase that the `guest_responses` row still exists with `rating: null, text_consent: false, deleted_at: null` "so the anonymous lifetime aggregate remains rebuildable." Grepping implementations of `PrivacySubjectContributor` outside tests returns only this adapter, the port, and the lifecycle itself — there is no erase path that destroys aggregate inputs.

Second, the ordering the reviewer proposes would be the actual bug. The correction that must reach the lifetime aggregate for an erasure IS the delta produced by the erase (rating -> NULL, consent -> false). Running `deliverAggregateCorrections` before `erase` would deliver a no-op and the gate would pass vacuously — exactly the failure the reviewer ascribes to the current code. Running it after, inside the same `runInTransaction` (privacy-request-lifecycle.ts:234 and 271, so the erase's writes are visible to the delivery), is the only order that can see anything to deliver. Same for `correct`/`withdraw`: operation first, then deliver.

Third, the contract is not inverted. privacy-request-lifecycle.ts:208-214 reads "1. apply the contributor operation; 2. deliver the resulting corrections; 3. only THEN purge source facts and append the backup-erasure ledger entry" — "the RESULTING corrections" presupposes the operation already ran, and step 3 pairs the purge with the backup-erasure ledger append. The code is contributor op (265) -> deliver + gate (271-279) -> appendLedgerEntry (282-295), i.e. 1 -> 2 -> 3 verbatim. The test assertion ['guest.erase','deliverAggregateCorrections','appendLedgerEntry'] (test:270-274) pins the correct order, not a wrong one.

At most there is a documentation nit: the module header at lines 3-9 says source facts are "purged" on erasure, which reads stronger than what `erase` actually does and is what misled the reviewer. That is wording, not a defect — no reachable execution loses an erased subject's contribution from `portal_metric_lifetime_aggregates`.

The claim assumes the registry's counsel-approval gate was ever meant to govern the RETENTION_RULES sweep. The code and its docs say the opposite, explicitly, in three places.

1. src/shared/db/retention/retention-registry.ts:6-8 — "It is DECLARATIVE. It does not execute; the separately authorized `RETENTION_RULES` sweep does that, and this registry is the governance layer above it."

2. docs/operations/retention-registry.md:19-24 — "It is declarative. It does not execute. The scheduled sweep (src/shared/jobs/retention-sweep.job.ts) executes a separate, separately authorized rule set; the registry sits above it as the governance layer." Lines 24-35 add "Do not read a registry row as a description of live behaviour" and define the two fields: `eligibility.horizon` = what counsel approves (notice-facing default), `eligibility.implementedBoundary` = what the shipped code already enforces today. The reviewer's central "contradiction" (header says report-only, yet implementedBoundary says "Live: ... deletes") is exactly the distinction that schema exists to make; the doc names conflating them as the failure mode it prevents.

3. The same doc, lines 49-53, states the gate's actual scope verbatim: "createRetentionSweepHandler refuses any registry rule handed to it through registryApplyRules, before it opens a single evidence row." That is precisely what retention-sweep.job.ts:319-322 does, and the dep's JSDoc (lines 279-287) says the refusal lives at that boundary because handing registry rules to the scheduled sweep "is exactly how report-only quietly becomes apply." It is a tripwire against a future caller wiring registry rules into the sweep — not a claim that RETENTION_RULES is subject to it.

The behaviour called a defect is asserted as intended by a test the reviewer did not read: src/shared/jobs/retention-sweep.job.test.ts, "runs the separately authorized sweep rules when no registry rule is handed in" (executeRetentionRule called once), paired with "refuses a pending-counsel registry rule before opening any evidence row (LIF-01-T16)". The sweep is BQC-1.6 production-scheduled retention that predates the LIF-01-T16 registry (retention-sweep.job.ts:1-9). The registry was added as governance documentation over already-live behaviour, and each subject the reviewer names carries an implementedBoundary saying so ("Live: the scheduled subject guest_responses.deidentified_fact deletes on retention_deadline", etc.). Whether counsel should also sign off on pre-existing shipped deletions is a policy question the repo consciously documented — not an unguarded code path, a regression, or a gate that fails open.

The gate function itself is correct (retention-registry.ts:654-660): with the union 'pending_counsel' | 'approved', the early return fires only for approved rules and everything else throws. No inversion.

Residual observation only: no production caller currently passes registryApplyRules, so the guard is a dormant tripwire rather than an active check — a design/ergonomics note, and by the module's own account its intended shape.

Refuted on two independent grounds.

ORGANIZATION_LIFECYCLE_CONTEXTS is 17 entries (organization-lifecycle.ts:39-57); runPhase fires an unbounded Promise.all over all 17 (advance-organization-lifecycle.ts:142); all 16 non-Identity contributors are the shared scaffold whose run() opens deps.db.transaction (organization-lifecycle-receipt-store.ts:176) and takes .for('update') on the same organizationLifecycleAuthority row (:221), and Identity's own contributor also opens deps.db.transaction (identity-organization-lifecycle-contributor.ts:110). src/shared/db/index.ts:10 is drizzle(getPool()), so each transaction is a genuine pool.connect() against POOL_MAX_CONNECTIONS = 10, and src/worker/index.ts runs the default (4), background (3) and domain-events (20) workers in ONE process sharing that pool — so the starvation target is real, not hypothetical. worker.test.ts:42-49 only multiplies two constants and structurally cannot observe a 17-client job, so the reviewer is right that the pinning test is blind to this. The reviewer actually under-sold one point: because all 17 contend on the SAME authority row under FOR UPDATE, the fan-out buys zero parallelism — at most one contributor does work at a time while up to 10 hold pool clients. It is pure cost. The repo already has the correct remedy pattern for exactly this shape: src/contexts/review/infrastructure/exact-current-apply-admission.ts budgets a nested-transaction fan-out against POOL_MAX_CONNECTIONS with a process-wide semaphore, explicitly reasoning that independent budgets could collectively consume the pool. So this is a genuine, fixable design defect against a documented, load-bearing invariant ('background queue — single-client maintenance sweeps', WORST_CASE_POOL_CLIENTS_PER_JOB = 2).

Severity is medium rather than high, for three reasons the claim acknowledges only partly. (1) The path is unreachable in every current composition, not merely quarantined: src/composition/organization-export-contributors.ts:112-125 states createContainer deliberately supplies no lifecycle contributors, so organizationLifecycleCoordinator is null (build.ts:470-481), deps.advance is undefined, and the job handler short-circuits to {configured:false}; the schedule is also registration:'quarantined'. Arming requires an explicitly reviewed composition. (2) Even when armed the blast radius is bounded and non-corrupting: receipts are idempotent and the existing-receipt early return precedes the FOR UPDATE, so already-completed contributors neither take the row lock nor redo work, and transitions are CAS'd — a lock_timeout pass loses no data and converges across passes. (3) The error handling is less blind than claimed: the bare `catch { counts.failed += 1 }` does discard the error, but the job throws organizationLifecycleJobError('context_contribution_failed') whenever failed > 0, so the failure is signalled — what is lost is the diagnostic detail, which is a real but secondary issue. Two minor imprecisions in the claim: the pool is per-process and the API runs separately, so HTTP requests are not starved (only co-resident default/domain-events jobs are); and the 17-way fan-out is per candidate inside a sequential for-loop, not literally one 17-client hold for the whole pass, though with up to 50 candidates the pressure is effectively continuous. Net: not refuted — a bounded-admission gate (or simply sequential execution, since the row lock serializes anyway) should land before this coordinator is ever armed.

The reviewer's mechanical observations are accurate (the Closure Center evaluates no capability; getStore() at beta-capabilities.ts:452 is the sole web-process restore-isolation seam), but the defect conclusion fails on four independent grounds.

(1) The capability seam is not, and is not documented to be, a universal write fence. entry-point-catalogue.ts contains 46 rows with capability 'none', including registerUserAndOrg, registerMember, acceptInvitation, signInUser and setActiveOrganization -- all DB mutations that already write under RESTORE_MODE=isolated by design. You cannot even authenticate to reach the Closure Center without one of them writing. restore-mode.ts:12-16 is scoped precisely to "capability-gated server functions/mutations/external effects are impossible", and the pinned log line is "external effects disabled". The reviewer substituted a stronger "mutations impossible" posture that the code never claims. The Closure Center belongs to an existing catalogued class, not a new gap.

(2) No external effect is produced. assertRestoreModeCompatible(env,'worker') (restore-mode.ts:96-103) makes the worker refuse to boot, so there is no outbox relay, no BullMQ consumer and no schedule; a closure request commits a local row only.

(3) The restore scenario is not tenant-reachable. docs/operations/bqr6-recovery-rehearsal.md step 3.4 specifies a "no-domain signed-image web verifier"; the environment is operator-only via tunnel, and step 3.2 already grants that same operator direct psql access to the sibling. Triggering the claimed write additionally requires an AccountAdmin session, a valid reason code, a valid supportEvidenceRef and typing the exact Organization name (organization-closure-fns.ts:226) -- a deliberate operator act strictly weaker than access the drill already confers.

(4) The kill-switch half is the design intent, not a bug. All four commands share one gate decision; restoring the capability gate makes cancel/reactivate unreachable the moment the org-suspension fence engages -- exactly the deadlock the carve-out exists to prevent. The residual behaviour (an org's own AccountAdmin closing their own org while the emergency stop is engaged, authorised under FOR UPDATE on member+binding at organization-lifecycle-command-store.ts:88-113) is no escalation, no cross-tenant exposure and no external effect. The "unrecoverable" aggravation is speculative and rests on a separate finding.

The carve-out is also governed rather than accidental: all 14 closure rows in the catalogue (lines 1093-1340) carry an explicit reviewed note stating this decision verbatim.

The only genuine residue is a documentation nuance: the header's "not weaker ... it is stronger" is true along the authorisation axis and silent about the global-stop axis. That is a comment-precision nit; no code behaves incorrectly.

Confirmed as stated, at low severity. advance-property-erase.job.ts:78 opens the single `deps.runInTransaction`, and purgeContexts is called inside it at line 119 with `store = deps.storeIn(tx)`. In the real store (property-erase-command-store.ts), `withTx(tx) => build(tx, db)` binds every method — including recordContextReceipt (line 231) and completedContexts (line 247) — to that same runner, so contributor deletes and receipt inserts commit or roll back together. A crash, redeploy, or lost connection mid-pass therefore discards the receipts along with the deletes, and the next pass re-runs all 16 contexts. The file header (lines 10-13) and the port doc (property-erase-contributor.port.ts lines 9-11) both promise "resumes from the receipts rather than re-running contexts that already answered", which contradicts the dep doc 26 lines below at line 39 ("One transaction per pass; a throw leaves no partial receipt"). Consequently the `done` set (line 130) and the `outstanding` partial-pass branch (lines 156-172) are unreachable with the real store.

I tried hard to refute: completedContexts does NOT filter by outcome (no_data counts as answered), so no hidden reachability there; recordContextReceipt's ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING still runs on the tx runner; the guest contributor's erase(tx, scope) uses the passed tx, not a separate connection. The two tests that appear to cover resumption do not: advance-property-erase.job.test.ts:159 injects `existingReceipts` into an in-memory fake, and :208 stubs recordContextReceipt to a no-op — neither state is producible by the real store during a purge.

Reviewer overstated two details: there are 16 contexts, not 17 (PROPERTY_ERASE_CONTEXTS), and the ledger under-reporting sub-claim (erasedRowCount: rowsErased, line 191) is contingent on the unreachable multi-pass path, so no under-report occurs today. The job is also not yet wired into any scheduler, and behavior is safe regardless (the purge stays atomic; re-running is just wasted work). So this is a documentation/design-intent mismatch plus effectively dead defensive code, not a runtime bug — low, not higher.

The SQL ordering the reviewer quotes is real (property-erase-command-store.ts:136-148 orders `(state='purging') DESC, state_changed_at ASC LIMIT 1`), there is no attempts column, and advance-property-erase.job.ts:78 wraps the whole pass in one transaction so a throwing contributor discards the pass. But the filed defect does not hold:

(1) Unreachable by explicit design, not oversight. advancePropertyErase has no caller outside tests, and the sole documented entry point, scripts/ops/property-erase.ts, hard-refuses every mutating mode including `advance` with "erase execution is not armed in this build ... composition is pending". docs/operations/backup-and-lifecycle.md repeats this under a "Not yet armed" heading and lists what is outstanding: only 2 of 16 contributors exist, plus "the container composition and the job registration are pending". Scheduling/retry policy is part of that pending composition.

(2) The `purging`-wins precedence is a load-bearing safety invariant, and the suggested fix contradicts it. The domain table in property-erase.ts has `purging: ['purged']` and refuses cancel past the boundary with `irreversible_state`. Parking a stuck `purging` authority to work on another Property means starting a second irreversible erasure while one Property is half-destroyed. There is "no state to park it in" precisely because that outcome is refused by design.

(3) The failure direction is fail-safe: a stall erases nothing. The consequence is a delayed erasure requiring operator attention, not loss or corruption. The intended trigger per the CLI usage block is an operator-invoked `advance --apply` pass, so a failure surfaces to the operator immediately rather than looping silently.

(4) A stuck row is already detectable without an attempts column: only `transition` updates `state_changed_at`, so a stuck `purging` row has a pinned `state_changed_at`/`purge_started_at`, and nextAdvanceable already orders by that column.

(5) Partial progress is not generally blocked — the `outstanding.length > 0` branch (job lines 160-172) commits receipts and resumes next pass, covered by the "replays from persisted receipts after an interruption" and "does not complete or ledger a partial pass" tests. Only a deterministically throwing contributor produces the scenario.

What remains is a low-severity note for whoever arms the path: add a stuck-`purging` alert (none exists in src/shared/observability/alert-definitions.ts) and define the operator procedure for a deterministically failing contributor. Not a medium defect in landed code.

The reviewer's factual observations check out: GATE_F_ENGINEERING_ROLES (gate-f-approval-envelope.ts:54) has zero consumers repo-wide; roleKeyMapSchema (lines 130-144) has no superRefine or cross-role distinctness constraint; createGateFApprovalVerifier (236-277) only matches envelope.publicKeySha256 against roleKeys.roles[envelope.role].publicKeySha256 and never compares approverIdentity to custodian; gateFEvidenceSchema.superRefine (gate-f-evidence.ts:204-231) enforces role set/order but not identity or key distinctness; and the only distinctness test (gate-f-approval-envelope.test.ts:203) asserts over fixture-generated keys, not the production map.

But the severity framing is wrong. The exploit requires writing a duplicate enrolment into security/gate-f-approval-roles.json — a tracked, reviewed file where all six roles are currently not_enrolled with distinct named custodians. Anyone able to make that unreviewed edit has a strictly easier path: enrol their own fresh key under `counsel`, which is distinct from every other enrolled key and would sail past any distinctness constraint. The guard the reviewer demands therefore does not close the attack they describe; it only catches honest copy-paste/lazy enrolment.

The JSON's claim that "role separation is enforced structurally by the signed payload's role field" is accurate as written: `role` is in GATE_F_APPROVAL_SIGNED_FIELDS, so an operations envelope cannot be replayed as counsel; it only degrades under a duplicate enrolment the per-role custodian design presupposes away.

The approverIdentity sub-claim is weak: approverIdentity is inside the signed payload, so only the enrolled key holder can attest a name; putting the operator's name on a counsel envelope requires counsel's private key, which by design never exists in the repo/CI/operator checkout. And LEGAL_SELF_APPROVAL_PROHIBITED is not absent from the Gate F chain — legal-revision-set-evidence.ts:224-228 rejects prohibited approver name/organization on counsel-owned documents, and Gate F binds legalRevisionSetSha256 into the exact payload approvers sign (gate-f-evidence.ts:242-251).

What genuinely remains: a dead exported constant whose comment asserts a rule nothing enforces, and a missing operator-error guard (key/identity distinctness across roles) on a separation-of-duties control that currently fails closed anyway (zero keys enrolled). Worth fixing as hardening/dead-code cleanup, not a high-severity authorization bypass.

Mechanics partly confirmed but the defect framing is refuted. I ran the real CLI: a junk --plan-file with a self-computed planSha256 does produce a passed artifact (exit 0). However: (1) The claimed consequence — that the plan→authorize→execute separation "collapses into one self-attested invocation" — is not caused by the missing plan schema check. authorization.json is an unsigned operator-authored file, and rehearse-recovery.ts:260 requires authorization.operator === --operator, so the executing operator IS the authorizer. The same operator can run --plan, hash the genuine output, and self-authorize in one script; the plan bytes never influence the emitted evidence, so the junk path and the legitimate path yield identical artifacts. Validating --plan-file would restore no security property against the only actor who can reach this code. (2) The "leaves no trace" claim is factually wrong. I ran a second variant where the read-back names the plan digest as restore.reviewedRestorePlan.sha256 and the authorization digest as restore.reviewedPlanApproval.sha256: both files were written to the dependency dir (verified: "AUTH retained? true", "plan digest retained? true") without being in --inputs-dir. That is exactly why rehearse-recovery.ts:304-308 supplies them — recoveryRehearsalDependencyDigests already forces reviewedRestorePlan/reviewedPlanApproval retention on both paths, so Gate F does see the plan and the authorization under the intended wiring. The reviewer mistook a conditional drop for an unconditional one. (3) No documented promise is broken: recovery-rehearsal-plan.ts:8-13 and docs/operations/backup-and-lifecycle.md:196-197 claim only that --apply refuses unless the authorization's planSha256 equals the digest of the supplied plan file (an edited plan invalidates its own approval), which is true and covered by the existing test at rehearse-recovery.test.ts:287-294. What genuinely survives is a low-severity hardening gap: nothing enforces that the evidence's reviewed-plan/approval references equal the plan/authorization digests, and the plan's candidate is never compared with the --observations candidate, so an honest cross-candidate mixup is caught only downstream by Gate F's candidate-to-manifest binding. That is a hardening opportunity in a procedural, unsigned operator control, not a high-severity defect.

The headline defect ("an open blocking counsel decision does not block the gate") is refuted by controls the reviewer did not read. The Gate F bundle requires release.legalRevisionSet alongside release.legalApprovalChecklist (gate-f-evidence.ts:437-453 dispatches it to parseLegalRevisionSetEvidence with DEFAULT_LEGAL_REVISION_SET_CONTEXT = the compiled LEGAL_DOCUMENT_REGISTRY). legal-revision-set-evidence.ts:215 rejects any entry whose status is not 'approved', and REGISTRY_MIRRORED_FIELDS (line 175) forces status/version/digest/dates to mirror the registry row verbatim. So the reviewer's scenario — every tracked counsel decision open with blocksDocuments ['privacy-notice'] while the Gate F bundle validates — requires the registry to mark privacy-notice 'approved', which is precisely what approvalBlockingDecisionErrors rejects (counsel-decision-checklist.ts:308-322) via scripts/review/legal-document-registry.ts:113, wired into CI as pnpm check:legal-registry inside lint:ci (package.json:30, .github/workflows/ci.yml:95). Today the lock is total: all five registry rows are 'draft', and validateCounselDecisionChecklist (line 236-244) requires at least one open item per category, so no Gate F bundle can validate at all against the shipped default — the Gate F tests must inject an approved-registry fixture (gate-f-complete-evidence.test-fixtures.ts:308-309). Two supporting sub-claims also fail: the checklist is not unsigned self-attestation, since its digest is inside gateFDecisionDocument (gate-f-evidence.ts:329-340) which counsel signs under a fail-closed Ed25519 verifier (line 617-624); and the absence of a producer script is documented design (docs/release-evidence/review/rel-01-producer-implementation-2026-08-28.md:49, "authored by counsel, validated by release:validate-evidence"). What survives is only the reviewer's narrow factual observation: checklistItemIds (line 135) and sourceDocumentId (line 134) are unresolved free strings — a typo'd or fabricated id is silently accepted, and sourceDocumentId is loose where documents[].documentId is an enum over the same id space. That is a traceability/strictness hardening opportunity inside an already counsel-signed attestation, not the claimed gate bypass, so I rate the surviving residue low rather than medium.

The claim's core consequence -- that a canary window can pass while release identity continuity went unverified -- is refuted by the mandatory release_drift signal. `release_drift` is one of the nine REQUIRED signal categories enforced by the evidence schema (src/shared/release/canary-window-evidence.ts:16-26), and security/rel-01-canary-threshold-profile.json binds it as `canary-release-drift`, source `release_controller`, pointer `/identityMismatches`, comparator eq 0. It is fail-closed twice: scripts/release/observe-canary-window.ts:441-455 refuses to start the window when no `release_controller` endpoint is configured, and an unreadable or unresolvable read becomes a MISSING sample which forces `outcome: 'failed'`. So `continuity.releaseIdentityMismatches` is an opportunistic cross-check layered on top of a thresholded, non-optional drift signal, not the sole assurance the `passing` predicate rests on.

The reviewer's source analysis is also partly wrong. `/api/health/ready` is the `external_synthetic` source, and that branch never parses the response body through `identityFrom`/`configurationHeadFrom` at all -- createCanarySampleReader short-circuits at observe-canary-window.ts:180-200 and synthesizes its own probe rawSample. The readiness snapshot's shape is therefore irrelevant to either counter. `/api/health/metrics` returns the full OperationsSnapshot, which does expose top-level `release: { sha }` and `versions` (src/shared/health/operations-snapshot.ts:431-439), so the releaseSha half and the configuration head are in fact compared on every sample of three profile signals at 60s intervals.

The `configurationHeadMismatches` half of the claim is directly contradicted by the code: canary-sampler.ts:264-272 refuses to emit the artifact at all when no configuration head was ever observed (test at canary-sampler.test.ts:152-161), so "a single source suffices" is the intended semantic -- continuity of one authoritative head across the window, which is exactly what "drifted mid-window" means.

The only accurate part is that `releaseManifestSha256` is never compared through the two non-overridable sources. But that is by construction, not oversight: the candidate's manifest digest is the digest of a local promotion-manifest.json, and no runtime surface anywhere in the repo reports such a value (grep for manifestSha256 across src/shared/health and src/routes finds nothing). The reader type documents identity as present "when the source exposes it". The manifest-to-deployment binding is verified by other producers -- the CLI hashes the manifest file and refuses a declared-digest mismatch (observe-canary-window.ts:369-384), and promotion-readback-evidence.ts:308-322 requires an observed active image digest with no legacy SOURCE_REVISION override. The residual issue is prose only: docs/operations/immutable-release-promotion.md:616-617 claims a drifted RELEASE_MANIFEST_SHA256 increments the counter, which is reachable only via an operator-supplied source that volunteers release.manifestSha256. That is a documentation nit, not a defect that produces a wrong result.

Confirmed by execution. I built the repo's own complete Gate F bundle fixture, simulated a post-approval edit of docs/legal/privacy-notice.md (registry digest A=79447ca4…, on-disk digest B=81ac0bf6…), rewrote only the checklist's documents[privacy-notice].sha256 to B, rebuilt the bundle (index/decision digests and all six signatures regenerate), and passed a document reader returning B. validateGateFEvidenceBundle returned ok:true. The control case (checklist still claiming A, disk holding B) correctly failed with "on-disk digest … does not match the approved …", proving the only thing separating pass from fail is which digest the checklist happens to record.

Mechanism is exactly as claimed: parseLegalRevisionSetEvidence compares entry.sha256 only to the compiled registry row (legal-revision-set-evidence.ts:192-194) and cannot read files; its second digest pin (lines 251-254) applies only to IN_PRODUCT_NOTICES, and privacy-notice / internal-beta-agreement / google-access-disclosure are not in that list (legal-link-targets.ts:103-130). parseLegalApprovalChecklist compares only to readDocument(path) (legal-approval-checklist.ts:275-303). The single cross-artifact check at gate-f-evidence.ts:742-756 compares legalRevisionSetSha256 only, even though the documentId sets are identical (LEGAL_CHECKLIST_DOCUMENTS vs LEGAL_PUBLICATION_DOCUMENT_IDS), so a per-document comparison is trivially available and simply absent.

Reachability is real: scripts/release/validate-bundle.ts:84-100 exposes --legal-root explicitly so a reviewer can validate against a different document tree, while the revision set is checked against the compiled-in LEGAL_DOCUMENT_REGISTRY of the validating checkout; nothing requires the two to agree. Test coverage gap confirmed: the fixture derives checklist digests and registry rows from the same bytes (gate-f-complete-evidence.test-fixtures.ts:260-268 with legal-revision-set-evidence.test-fixtures.ts:80-95), so divergence is unrepresentable in tests, and gate-f-evidence.test.ts:565-573 is the only cross-check assertion.

Mitigation exists but is external and partial: pnpm check:legal-registry (package.json:30,129 -> validateLegalDocumentRegistry, legal-approval-authority.ts:120-128) does catch "approved document changed after approval", but only for the repo checkout's own docs/legal tree, as a separate lint:ci job, not as part of bundle validation, and it cannot cover a --legal-root pointed elsewhere.

Fairness correction to the reviewer's framing: counsel's envelope binds gateFDecisionSha256, which transitively covers the checklist artifact and therefore digest B, so it is not strictly true that counsel signs nothing about B. What is missing for B is any approval provenance — approved status, external-counsel approver, approvedAt, expiresOn, approvalEvidenceRef all attach to A. The bundle is internally self-contradictory and still validates, contradicting the stated guarantees at legal-revision-set-evidence.ts:22-23 and gate-f-evidence.ts:140-146. Medium is the right severity: an evidence/governance integrity hole, not a product-runtime vulnerability, and partly backstopped by a separate CI job.
